questions.topic: The constraint a viol's tuning imposes

stimulus.body: The working note below records the evidence for a claim about the constraint a viol's tuning imposes. the key, "Frets fixed to temperament", is the only choice consistent with that relation. A reader must decide which of the four proposed statements the note warrants, without using outside knowledge.

questions.stem: The prompt gives “Identify viol tuning constraint / Fretted. / The constraint a viol's tuning imposes” as the nudge. Which option is really supported?

options.misconception: mistakes a surface feature of "Equal temperament only, wrong" for the governing rule
substitutes a familiar but inapplicable case for the relation the passage establishes
selects "Scordatura forbidden, irrelevant" where the rule in the passage requires a different condition

questions.explanation: Fixed frets. The key, "Frets fixed to temperament", is the only choice consistent with that relation. "Equal temperament only, wrong" is tempting because it rests on a misreading of the concept, but it does not follow from the figures given. "No frets, denies" is tempting because it rejects a feature that is actually present, but it contradicts the value stated in the case. "Scordatura forbidden, irrelevant" is tempting because it points to a feature that has no bearing on the result, but it applies the rule to the wrong quantity.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The total span of a viol's tuning

stimulus.body: A short reference note on the total span of a viol's tuning is set for a close-reading task. It states: The key, "Two octaves", is the only choice consistent with that relation. Four statements are then offered, and only one of them follows from what the note actually says.

questions.stem: The note is checked against “Identify viol tuning span / Two. / The total span of a viol's tuning”. Which option survives that check?

options.misconception: reverses the direction of the reasoning the passage sets out
treats "One octave, too small" as if it followed from the evidence
selects "One and a half, undercounts" where the rule in the passage requires a different condition

questions.explanation: Two octaves. The key, "Two octaves", is the only choice consistent with that relation. "One octave, too small" is tempting because it chooses a value smaller than the one the calculation gives, but it contradicts the value stated in the case. "One and a half, undercounts" is tempting because it omits part of the quantity the figure actually contains, but it applies the rule to the wrong quantity. "Three octaves, overcounts" is tempting because it adds units that the figure does not contain, but it breaks the relation the case establishes.
